comment: Advocate presents the trial menu as co-equal with sunitinib at first recurrence, but NCCN GIST v1.2026 and ESMO 2022 still sequence sunitinib ahead of olverembatinib, belzutifan, and the FGFR agents, which sit in off-guideline trial-territory until their readouts mature. The Boikos 2016 figure (18% vs 2% on imatinib) is the consensus opening move; the newer agents earn that slot only once a trial confirms them. I would keep sunitinib as the labeled first reach rather than one option among equals.

Putting sunitinib first at recurrence is exactly where NCCN GIST v1.2026 and ESMO 2022 land for this subtype, and the MGMT-gating before temozolomide keeps the off-guideline alkylator honest. The toxicity-first ordering tracks the guideline sequence rather than fighting it, so there is nothing for me to qualify on guideline-fit. Sunitinib over imatinib here rests on the same Boikos 2016 figures, 18% versus 2%, that ESMO cites.

Critic reads the 18% sunitinib response (Boikos 2016) as directional rather than dependable, but that retrospective figure is precisely the evidence ESMO 2022 weighed when it preferred sunitinib over imatinib in this subtype. The guideline preference is collective expert calibration of the same data the critic is discounting, not a separate claim that has to outrank it. On that basis I would keep sunitinib at the front of the contingency ladder.

Rogaratinib's 41.7% (PMID 42191879) is a real signal, but a single-arm n=24 cohort closed to accrual appears in neither NCCN GIST v1.2026 nor ESMO 2022, so ranking it first puts a pre-guideline number ahead of the consensus surveillance-then-sunitinib path. NCCN does endorse clinical-trial enrollment for SDH-deficient GIST, so the FGFR bet belongs on the trial menu at recurrence, not at the head of the plan while the patient is NED. The guideline-aligned move now is to confirm the dSDH phenotype and bank trial eligibility, not to lead with an agent no society has yet adopted.
